findings: The ordinary 2026–2027 curriculum closes at 60 EC each year. Entry preparation and original-language progression do not convert into extra credits. The first option sustains classical study through translated literature, myth, rhetoric, philosophy, archaeology and reception. The second has direct ancient content in archaeology, political philosophy, empire, myth and Athenian democracy, with political and legal comparisons across periods. Renaissance art adds visual and historical context, while comparative private law has a supporting role only. Eleven courses and 82.5 EC differ each way. The timetable passes after moving Rhetoric in Action and Renaissance art and replacing European Union Law in the second option.

The actual Great Literary Works evidence supports the bounded classical literature match through translated epic and tragedy. It does not recreate the dedicated Euripides and translation course. Creative writing and adaptation training leave the combined Classics reception requirement visible as a distinct component. Greek and Latin acquisition, linguistic analysis and original-language study lack a coherent UCR counterpart.
